response.consequence: An attacker who has a password and one backup code can use that code more than once by racing requests. A consumed backup code can also become valid again. This breaks the single-use guarantee of 2FA backup codes.
response.explanation: The user row, including the encrypted backupCodes, is read once at the top of authorize. The code decrypts it, finds the index, sets that entry to null, re-encrypts, and calls prisma.user.update with `where: { id }` only. There is no transaction, no row lock, and no compare-and-set on the previous backupCodes value. Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code both read the same unconsumed list, both find the code, and both pass. Each then writes back its own copy, so the last write wins. A concurrent login using a different backup code can also overwrite the first login's nulling, which revives the code that was just consumed. I checked the indexOf concern: the stored entries are nulled and the input is a non-empty string, so it cannot match a nulled entry.

response.explanation: Line 121 only verifies the password when `!credentials.totpCode`. Nothing later checks it. A request with an email, an arbitrary non-empty totpCode, no password and a valid backupCode skips the password check. It then enters the new backup-code branch (line 131), which doesn't look at totpCode, and succeeds. A request with a valid totpCode and no password is also accepted by the existing TOTP branch. response.consequence: A backup code that is meant to be single-use can be redeemed more than once. In a race, a code that was already used can also become valid again. This weakens the one-time guarantee of the second-factor recovery codes.
response.explanation: In authorize(), the backup-code branch reads user.backupCodes in the earlier findUnique, checks the code with indexOf, then writes back the whole re-encrypted array with prisma.user.update. The update has no condition that the stored backupCodes are unchanged. Two concurrent login requests with the same valid backup code both read the old array, both find the code, and both succeed. The update only nulls the one entry, so the second write does not restore the code, but both sessions are issued. The same pattern would also lose updates if two different codes are used at once: the later write re-enables the earlier consumed code, because it writes back an array that still holds it. The rate limiter reduces how easily this can be triggered, but it does not make the consumption atomic.
response.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so a single-use code can be replayed concurrently
